title: Impact of the British Rule on India

notes.subtopic: 1. Big Picture — From Traders to Rulers
notes.content:
**Executive summary:** By the end of the 18th century the English East India Company (EEIC) was no longer a mere trading company — it had become a formidable colonial power controlling most of India. Its policies changed Indian **agriculture, industry, transport and education**.

**Must know**
• To retain control, the British set up an administration for **law and order** and **internal security**.
• Land revenue was the **main source of state income**, so agriculture got special attention.
• Aim: make India a **supplier of cheap raw materials** to British industries and a **market** for British goods.

**Chapter map:** Land revenue settlements → Impact on peasants → Ruin of industries → Transport & communication → Economic drain → Anglicist–Orientalist debate → Macaulay's Minute → Wood's Despatch → Effects of Western education.

**Three systems — learn the table!**

| Settlement | Introduced by / Year | Region | Who paid the revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Permanent Settlement** | Lord Cornwallis, **1793** | Bengal, Bihar, Orissa | **Zamindars** — made owners of land; revenue fixed permanently |
| **Ryotwari Settlement** | Thomas Munro (Governor of Madras, 1820–27) | **Bombay and Madras Presidencies** | **Ryots** (cultivators) directly to the government |
| **Mahalwari Settlement** | 1820s–1830s | North India — mainly **Uttar Pradesh and Punjab** | The **mahal** (village / group of villages) through the village headman |

**Why introduced?** To maximise and secure land revenue — the main income of the Company — regardless of the hardship to peasants.

fiveW.why: Land revenue was the Company's main income — maximise and secure it
fiveW.how: Fixed revenue collected via zamindars, directly from ryots, or from the village (mahal)

notes.content:
**Features (common to all regions)**
• Created a **new class of landlords loyal to the British**.
• The Company got a **fixed revenue** without the trouble of collecting it from peasants itself.
• The new zamindari system encouraged **absentee landlordism** — owners lived far away and rented out land.
• A host of **intermediaries** grew between the state and the cultivator.
• A class of **corrupt moneylenders** emerged as intermediaries.

**Keyword — Absentee landlordism:** a person owns property and rents it out for profit but does not live in that region.

notes.subtopic: 4. Impact of the Settlements on Peasants
notes.content:
**The settlements were exploitative and oppressive.**
• **Land became a saleable commodity** — it could be bought, sold or mortgaged.
• Zamindars **squeezed peasants** for more tax and kept the extra for themselves.
• Revenue had to be paid **even during famines**; defaulters were **evicted**.
• Zamindars and the British were **indifferent** to peasant suffering.
• Frequent evictions created a **class of landless peasants**.
• Peasants borrowed from **moneylenders at high interest** → **cycle of debt**.
• **Over-cultivation** exhausted soil fertility → **regular famines**.

**Topper link:** Peasant misery → peasant revolts → one of the causes of the **Great Uprising of 1857** (Ch 9).

**Indian industries suffered a great setback.**
• Britain imposed **heavy duties on Indian textiles** entering Britain.
• British **machine-made goods entered India duty-free** or at a nominal duty.
• This **one-way free trade** made Indian goods costly and British goods cheap.
• Result: sales of Indian artisans and weavers fell sharply → **loss of livelihood** → **ruin of cottage industries**.
• India was turned from an exporter of finished goods into an **exporter of raw materials** (cotton, jute, indigo) and an **importer of finished goods**.

**Exam phrase:** *de-industrialisation* of India.

fiveW.who: British government vs Indian artisans and weavers
fiveW.why: To sell British machine-made goods and buy cheap raw materials
fiveW.how: Heavy duties on Indian textiles in Britain; British goods duty-free in India (one-way free trade)

notes.content:
**Why built?** To consolidate British power — move troops fast, quell revolts, and carry raw materials to ports and finished goods inland.

**What was built:** metalled roads, canals and railways connecting cities, ports and agricultural centres.

**Key dates (1853):**
• **First railway line: Bombay to Thane (1853).**
• **Post and telegraph department** set up in the same year.
• **First telegraph line: Calcutta to Agra.**

**Benefits**
• Efficient governance and quick troop movement for the British.
• Easier movement of raw materials and finished goods.
• **Indian merchants** also profited from exporting cotton, jute, indigo.
• **Unintended result:** Indians from different regions met and communicated → **unity and nationalism** → which ultimately helped end British rule.

**Now:** Indian Railways is owned by the Government of India — over 1,10,000 km of track; India has 1.5 lakh+ post offices.

fiveW.what: Railways, roads, canals, post and telegraph
fiveW.why: Move troops, quell revolts, carry raw materials and goods
fiveW.how: Built a network linking cities, ports and farm centres — which also united Indians

notes.content:
**Forms of exploitation**
• Raw materials bought **cheap**; British manufactured goods sold **dear**, flooding Indian markets → ruin of cottage industries.
• **High taxes** on peasants → poverty and discontent → **peasant revolts**.
• Workers paid **low wages**; no effort to improve Indian industry or agriculture.
• **India's wealth was systematically drained to England.**

**Topper tip:** The idea of the *Drain of Wealth* was later argued by **Dadabhai Naoroji** — quoting him in a long answer adds value.

**Charter Act of 1813:** the Company had to spend **₹1 lakh annually** on the education of Indians. This sparked a debate in England on *what* to teach and *in which language*.

| Orientalists | Anglicists |
|---|---|
| Traditional Indian learning | Western learning |
| Medium: classical & regional Indian languages (Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian) | Medium: **English** |
| Favoured oriental scholarship | Led by **Thomas Macaulay** |

**Resolution:** **Lord William Bentinck** ended the debate by passing a resolution (1835) in favour of Western education in English.

fiveW.who: Orientalists vs Anglicists (led by Macaulay); decided by Lord William Bentinck
fiveW.what: Debate on the medium and content of Indian education
fiveW.why: Charter Act 1813 set aside ₹1 lakh a year for education
fiveW.how: Bentinck's resolution chose Western education in English

notes.content:
**Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835)**
• Thomas Macaulay — **Law Member of the Governor-General's Council**.
• **Condemned Indian languages** and did not encourage Indian forms of knowledge.
• Wanted a class of Indians to act as **interpreters/link between rulers and the ruled** — *"Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect."*
• This class would supply **cheap staff for lower levels of administration**.

**Wood's Despatch (1854)**
• Sent by **Charles Wood**, President of the **Board of Control**, to Governor-General **Lord Dalhousie**.
• Laid the **foundation of the modern system of education** in India (often called the *Magna Carta of English education in India*).
• Aim: promotion of **Western education**; **English** medium for higher education.
• English-medium schools; **girls' schools** and grants for women's education.
• **Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras — 1857.**

**Did you know?** **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay**, writer of *Vande Mataram*, was one of the first graduates of Calcutta University.

fiveW.who: Thomas Macaulay; Charles Wood → Lord Dalhousie
fiveW.why: Create an English-educated class of loyal clerks and interpreters
fiveW.how: English-medium schools, girls' schools, grants, three universities

notes.content:
| Negative effects | Positive effects |
|---|---|
| Complete **Westernisation** of the education system | **Awareness** of being under foreign rule |
| **Replaced indigenous** methods of education | Spread of ideas of **democracy, liberty and fraternity** |
| Created English-educated Indians who mostly became **low-ranking clerks** | **National consciousness** inspired by the French Revolution and American War of Independence |
| **Rejection of Indian culture**; preference for all things British | **English became a common language** — Indians of different regions shared problems and exposed ill-effects of British rule |

**Keywords:** Anglicists · Orientalists · Imperialist · Nationalist · Formidable · Absentee landlordism.

questions.question: Thomas Macaulay condemned the use of Indian languages in his Minute on Indian Education.
questions.answer: True. His 1835 Minute condemned Indian languages and did not encourage Indian forms of knowledge.

questions.question: Under the Permanent Settlement, the revenue to be paid by zamindars was revised every 30 years.
questions.answer: False. The revenue was fixed **permanently** — that is why it was called the Permanent Settlement.

questions.question: Peasants were excused from paying revenue during famines.
questions.answer: False. Peasants had to pay **even in famines**; defaulters were evicted.

questions.question: British machine-made goods entered India duty-free or at nominal cost.
questions.answer: True — part of the one-way free trade policy.

questions.question: The improved transport system benefited only the British.
questions.answer: False. Indian merchants profited too, and it helped unite Indians, fuelling nationalism.

questions.question: The Orientalists wanted education to be imparted in English.
questions.answer: False. The **Anglicists** wanted English; the Orientalists favoured classical and regional Indian languages.

questions.question: Wood's Despatch recommended English as the medium of instruction for higher education.
questions.answer: True.

questions.question: The Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were set up in 1857.
questions.answer: True — as per Wood's Despatch.

questions.question: Western education led to the growth of ideas of democracy, liberty and fraternity among educated Indians.
questions.answer: True — one of its positive effects.

questions.question: The British made great efforts to improve Indian industry and agriculture.
questions.answer: False. They made **no effort** to improve Indian industry or agriculture.

questions.question: What steps were taken by the British to improve transport in India?
questions.answer:
• Built an elaborate network of metalled roads, canals and railway lines connecting major cities, ports and agricultural centres.
  • Introduced the railway system — first line from Bombay to Thane (1853).
  • Set up the post and telegraph department (1853); first telegraph line from Calcutta to Agra.
questions.topperTip: Give the year 1853 and both routes — that's what separates a 2/2 answer from 1/2.

questions.question: Where was the first railway line inaugurated in India?
questions.answer: The first railway line was inaugurated in 1853 from Bombay to Thane.
questions.topperTip: Always pair a place with its year.

questions.question: Who was Charles Wood?
questions.answer: Charles Wood was the President of the Board of Control, a British official who oversaw the EEIC. In 1854 he sent the famous Wood's Despatch to Governor-General Lord Dalhousie, which laid the foundation of the modern system of education in India.
questions.topperTip: Don't stop at his post — add what he is famous for (the Despatch).

questions.question: Name the famous Bengali novelist who was one of the first graduates from Calcutta University.
questions.answer: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, writer of India's national song Vande Mataram.

questions.question: (Picture study) Name the university set up in the Bengal Presidency. When was it set up? Name two other universities established under Wood's Despatch.
questions.answer:
• (a) University of Calcutta.
  • (b) Set up in 1857.
  • (c) University of Bombay and University of Madras (both 1857).
questions.topperTip: Label each part (a), (b), (c) exactly as asked — examiners mark part-wise.

questions.question: Why were the land revenue settlements introduced by the British?
questions.answer:
• Land revenue was the main source of state income for the Company, so it wanted to maximise and secure it.
  • The British wanted India to be an agricultural supplier of cheap raw materials for industries in England.
  • They wanted a fixed, assured revenue without the trouble of collecting it from each peasant, and a class of landlords loyal to them.
questions.topperTip: Three reasons = three marks. Keep one reason per point.

questions.question: What were the features of the land revenue settlements?
questions.answer:
• Created a new social class of landlords loyal to the British.
  • The Company was assured a fixed revenue without the trouble of collecting it from peasants.
  • Encouraged absentee landlordism and created a host of intermediaries between the state and the cultivator.
  • A class of corrupt moneylenders emerged as intermediaries.

questions.question: What was the impact of the land revenue settlements on Indian peasants?
questions.answer:
• Land became a saleable commodity — bought, sold or mortgaged.
  • Zamindars pressurised peasants to pay more and kept the extra for themselves.
  • Revenue had to be paid even during famines; defaulters were evicted, creating a class of landless peasants.
  • Peasants borrowed from moneylenders at high interest and fell into a cycle of debt.
  • Over-cultivation depleted soil fertility, leading to regular famines.
questions.topperTip: End with a linking line: this discontent led to peasant revolts and contributed to the Revolt of 1857.

questions.answer:

questions.topperTip: A comparison question → always answer in a table. Same 'basis' rows for every column.

questions.question: 'Indian industries also suffered a great setback under the British colonial rule.' Do you support the statement? Give reasons.
questions.answer:
Yes, I support the statement.

  • The British imposed heavy duties on Indian textiles entering Britain.
  • British machine-made goods entered India duty-free or at nominal cost — a policy of one-way free trade.
  • Indian goods became costly and could not compete with cheap British goods; artisans and weavers lost sales and livelihoods.
  • Raw materials were bought cheap and finished goods sold dear, ruining cottage industries; the British made no effort to develop Indian industry.
questions.topperTip: HOTS 'do you support' → start with a clear Yes/No, then justify. Using the term 'de-industrialisation' impresses examiners.

questions.question: Which is true for the economic exploitation of India by the British? (a) Artisans lost livelihoods due to cheap British goods (b) Peasants paid high taxes, increasing poverty (c) Both a and b. Give a reason.
questions.answer:
(c) Both a and b.

  • Cheap machine-made British goods flooded Indian markets and ruined artisans.
  • High taxes on peasants increased poverty and discontent, leading to peasant revolts.
questions.topperTip: Give one reason for EACH part when the answer is 'both'.

questions.question: How did the improved transport system benefit the British?
questions.answer:
• Efficient governance — quick transport of troops and rapid communication to quell revolts and disturbances.
  • Easier transfer of raw materials to ports and finished goods to markets, promoting British trade and commerce.
  • Helped consolidate British power across India.

questions.question: 'The transport and communication system, built for imperialist designs, ultimately helped end British rule.' Explain.
questions.answer:
• Railways, roads, post and telegraph were built to move troops and goods and strengthen British control.
  • But they also benefited Indian merchants, who exported cotton, jute and indigo and grew wealthy.
  • They increased communication between Indians of different regions.
  • This infused a sense of unity and led to the growth of nationalism — which in due course brought an end to British rule.
questions.topperTip: Structure = Aim → Unintended effect → Final result. This 'irony' angle is a favourite HOTS question.

questions.question: Describe the forms of economic exploitation of India by the British.
questions.answer:
• Cheap raw materials, costly finished goods: Indian markets were flooded with British goods, ruining small-scale cottage industries.
  • High taxes on peasants increased poverty and discontent, causing peasant revolts.
  • Low wages for workers; no effort to improve industry or agriculture.
  • Drain of wealth: India's wealth was systematically drained away to England.
questions.topperTip: Mentioning Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Drain Theory' shows extra reading.

questions.question: What was the Anglicist–Orientalist debate? How was it resolved?
questions.answer:
• The Charter Act of 1813 required the Company to spend ₹1 lakh annually on Indian education, which sparked a debate in England on the education policy for India.
  • Orientalists wanted traditional learning in classical and regional Indian languages.
  • Anglicists, led by Thomas Macaulay, insisted on Western education with English as the medium.
  • Resolution: Lord William Bentinck ended the debate by passing a resolution (1835) in favour of Western education in English.
questions.topperTip: Cause (1813 Act) → Two sides → Outcome (Bentinck). Missing Bentinck costs a mark.

questions.question: What was Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education?
questions.answer:
• Written in 1835 by Thomas Macaulay, Law Member of the Governor-General's Council.
  • It condemned the use of Indian languages and did not encourage Indian forms of knowledge.
  • It proposed Western education through English across British territories.
  • Aim: to create a class of Indians who would be interpreters between the rulers and the ruled — "Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect" — and provide cheap staff for lower administration.
questions.topperTip: Quoting Macaulay's famous line in the answer is a guaranteed topper move.

questions.question: (Source-based) From Macaulay's Minute, what do you learn about his attitude towards the vernacular medium of education?
questions.answer:
• Macaulay considered Indian vernacular languages unfit to convey modern knowledge in their present form.
  • He wanted an English-educated class to first 'refine' and 'enrich' the vernaculars with Western scientific terms.
  • This shows a dismissive, superior attitude towards Indian languages and knowledge.
questions.topperTip: In source questions, quote a phrase from the passage ('refine the vernacular dialects') as evidence.

questions.question: Do you think the British were able to create a class of Indians who were 'Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect'?
questions.answer:
• Partly yes: an English-educated class did emerge; many became clerks and some rejected Indian culture in favour of all things British.
  • But the plan backfired: the same educated Indians learnt ideas of liberty, democracy and nationalism and became leaders of the national movement, using English to unite Indians against British rule.
questions.topperTip: Opinion questions reward a balanced 'yes, but' answer with evidence on both sides.

questions.question: What were the main recommendations of Wood's Despatch? How were they implemented?
questions.answer:
• Sent in 1854 by Charles Wood to Lord Dalhousie; laid the foundation of modern education in India.
  • Aim declared: promotion of Western education.
  • English to be the medium for higher education.
  • Implementation: English-medium schools were set up; girls' schools were brought under government control with grants for women's education; Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were set up in 1857.
questions.topperTip: Wood's Despatch is often called the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India' — add this line.

questions.question: Discuss three negative effects of Western education introduced by the British in India.
questions.answer:
• It led to the complete Westernisation of the educational system and replaced indigenous methods of education.
  • It created English-educated Indians who mostly became low-ranking clerks.
  • Westernised Indians rejected Indian culture and preferred all things British.

questions.question: State three positive effects of Western education in India.
questions.answer:
• Created awareness among Indians of being under foreign rule.
  • Spread ideas of democracy, liberty and fraternity; knowledge of the French Revolution and American War of Independence created national consciousness.
  • English became a common language, so Indians of different regions could share common problems and expose the ill-effects of British rule.

questions.question: Define: (a) Anglicists (b) Orientalists.
questions.answer:
• Anglicists: those who felt that education for Indians should be Western, with English as the medium of instruction.
  • Orientalists: those who argued for traditional Indian education in classical Indian languages.

questions.question: What is absentee landlordism? How did it harm peasants?
questions.answer: Absentee landlordism is when a person owns property and rents it out for profit but does not live in that region. Such landlords had no interest in the land or the tenants; a chain of intermediaries and moneylenders squeezed the peasants for more rent.

questions.question: How did different revenue settlements in different areas affect the life of the people of India? (Debate question)
questions.answer:
• Bengal (Permanent): zamindars became owners; peasants became mere tenants at the mercy of zamindars and faced eviction.
  • Bombay & Madras (Ryotwari): no zamindar, but the state itself became a huge landlord with very high, periodically raised demands.
  • North India (Mahalwari): whole villages were jointly responsible — devastating effects when crops failed.
  • Common result everywhere: debt to moneylenders, landless peasants, famines and discontent that fed into the Revolt of 1857.
questions.topperTip: Region-wise answer + one common conclusion = full marks on a debate/HOTS question.

questions.question: 'The British policies turned India into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods.' Justify.
questions.answer:
• Land revenue policies pushed peasants to grow cash crops such as cotton, jute and indigo for British industry.
  • Railways carried raw materials to ports and brought British goods to the interior.
  • One-way free trade made British goods cheap and Indian goods costly, so Indian markets were flooded with British manufactures.
questions.topperTip: Connect agriculture + transport + trade — linking three sub-topics shows chapter mastery.
